questions.stem: The mass number of an isotope tells you:
options: the number of electrons orbiting its nucleus
the number of protons plus neutrons in its nucleus
the number of protons in its nucleus only
the number of neutrons in its nucleus only
questions.explanation: The mass number A counts the nucleons, protons plus neutrons. The atomic number Z counts the protons, so the number of neutrons is A − Z. Uranium-238, for example, has 92 protons and 146 neutrons.

questions.stem: Which description of the strong nuclear force is correct?
options: It attracts nucleons to each other, but only over a range of about 10⁻¹⁵ m
It attracts nucleons to each other over any distance, falling as 1/r² like gravity
It repels protons from each other, which is why heavy nuclei are unstable
It acts only between protons, because neutrons have no electric charge
questions.explanation: The strong force acts between all nucleons, protons and neutrons alike, and is much stronger than the electrostatic force at nuclear distances. Its range is only a few femtometres, so a nucleon is held mainly by its nearest neighbours. Repulsion between protons is electrostatic.

questions.stem: Why do stable heavy nuclei have considerably more neutrons than protons?
options: The weak force turns every second proton into a neutron, so heavy nuclei end up with about twice as many neutrons
Neutrons are heavier than protons, so extra neutrons increase the gravitational attraction holding the nucleus together
Proton repulsion acts across the whole nucleus but the strong force only between neighbours, so neutrons add attraction
Neutrons repel each other strongly, so extra neutrons are needed to push the protons apart and keep the nucleus from collapsing
questions.explanation: Electrostatic repulsion has long range, so every proton repels every other proton, and the total repulsion grows quickly with Z. The strong force acts only between nearby nucleons. Extra neutrons add strong-force attraction without adding repulsion, so larger nuclei need a higher neutron-to-proton ratio to be stable.

questions.stem: Which type of radiation is the most ionising and the least penetrating?
options: Beta
Gamma
X-ray
Alpha
questions.explanation: Alpha particles are helium nuclei with a +2 charge and a large mass, so they ionise strongly and lose their energy quickly, being stopped by a sheet of paper or a few centimetres of air. Gamma rays are the least ionising and most penetrating.

questions.stem: Which row correctly compares the three types of nuclear radiation?
options: Alpha: helium nucleus, +2. Beta-minus: photon, 0. Gamma: electron, −1
Alpha: proton, +1. Beta-minus: neutron, 0. Gamma: electron, −1
Alpha: helium nucleus, +2. Beta-minus: electron, −1. Gamma: photon, 0
Alpha: electron, −1. Beta-minus: helium nucleus, +2. Gamma: photon, 0
questions.explanation: An alpha particle is two protons and two neutrons (charge +2), a beta-minus particle is a fast electron (charge −1) and gamma radiation is a high-energy photon with no charge or mass. Beta-plus particles are positrons, with charge +1.

questions.stem: Gamma radiation is emitted from a nucleus. What happens to the nucleus's mass number and atomic number?
options: The mass number falls by 4 and the atomic number by 2
The atomic number rises by 1; the mass number stays the same
The mass number falls by 1; the atomic number stays the same
Neither changes; the nucleus drops to a lower energy state
questions.explanation: A gamma photon has no charge and no mass, so it carries away energy only. The nucleus goes from an excited state to a lower-energy state of the same isotope. Gamma emission often follows alpha or beta decay, which leaves the daughter nucleus excited.

questions.stem: Uranium-238 (Z = 92) undergoes alpha decay. What is the daughter nucleus?
options: Protactinium-238, Z = 91
Thorium-234, Z = 90
Thorium-236, Z = 90
Radium-234, Z = 88
questions.explanation: An alpha particle carries away 4 nucleons and 2 protons, so A falls from 238 to 234 and Z from 92 to 90, which is thorium. Mass number and charge are both conserved: 238 = 234 + 4 and 92 = 90 + 2.

questions.stem: Strontium-90 (Z = 38) undergoes beta-minus decay. What is the daughter nucleus?
options: Yttrium-91, Z = 39
Yttrium-90, Z = 39
Rubidium-90, Z = 37
Strontium-89, Z = 38
questions.explanation: In beta-minus decay a neutron becomes a proton, emitting an electron and an antineutrino. Z rises by 1 to 39 (yttrium) and A stays at 90. Rubidium-90 would result from a decrease in Z, which happens in beta-plus decay.

questions.stem: Carbon-11 (Z = 6), a tracer used in some PET scans, decays by beta-plus emission. What is the daughter nucleus?
options: Carbon-10, Z = 6
Beryllium-7, Z = 4
Boron-11, Z = 5
Nitrogen-11, Z = 7
questions.explanation: In beta-plus decay a proton changes into a neutron, emitting a positron and a neutrino. Z falls by 1 to 5 (boron) and A stays at 11. Nitrogen-11 would need Z to rise, as in beta-minus decay, and beryllium-7 would need alpha decay.

questions.stem: What role does the weak force play in beta-minus decay?
options: It changes a down quark in a neutron into an up quark, turning the neutron into a proton
It binds an extra electron to the nucleus until the nucleus becomes unstable and ejects it
It pushes protons apart until one of them escapes the nucleus as a beta particle
It changes an up quark in a proton into a down quark, turning the proton into a neutron
questions.explanation: In beta-minus decay the weak force changes the flavour of a quark: a neutron (udd) becomes a proton (uud), emitting an electron and an electron antineutrino. The reverse change, a proton becoming a neutron, happens in beta-plus decay. Electrons are created in the decay, not stored in the nucleus.

questions.stem: Which quantities are conserved in every nuclear decay and transmutation?
options: Charge only, because nucleons can be destroyed
Rest mass only, because energy is converted to mass
The number of protons and the number of neutrons separately
Charge and nucleon number, along with mass-energy
questions.explanation: In a balanced nuclear equation the charges (atomic numbers) and nucleon numbers (mass numbers) are equal on both sides, and total mass-energy is conserved. Rest mass alone is not conserved, since some becomes kinetic energy, and protons and neutrons can change into each other in beta decay.

questions.stem: Nitrogen-14 (Z = 7) is struck by an alpha particle, and a proton is emitted. What nucleus is produced in this transmutation?
options: Oxygen-18, Z = 8
Fluorine-18, Z = 9
Carbon-14, Z = 6
Oxygen-17, Z = 8
questions.explanation: Balance the nucleons: 14 + 4 = A + 1, so A = 17. Balance the charge: 7 + 2 = Z + 1, so Z = 8, which is oxygen. This reaction, observed by Rutherford, was the first artificial transmutation.

questions.stem: The half-life of a radioisotope is:
options: the time for a single nucleus to lose half of its mass
the time for half of the radioactive nuclei in a sample to decay
half of the time it takes for every nucleus in a sample to decay
the time for the mass of a sample to fall to zero
questions.explanation: Half-life is the time for the number of undecayed nuclei, and so the activity, to halve. Decay is random, so a sample never decays completely in a definite time, and one nucleus either decays or does not.

questions.stem: A sample contains 80 g of a radioisotope with a half-life of 5.0 days. How much of the isotope remains undecayed after 15 days?
options: 0 g
questions.explanation: 15 days is three half-lives, so the amount halves three times: 80 → 40 → 20 → 10 g. Treating the decay as linear would give 0 g after a fixed time, but radioactive decay is exponential.

questions.stem: Technetium-99m has a half-life of 6.0 hours. What fraction of a dose remains after 24 hours?
questions.explanation: 24 hours is four half-lives, so the fraction remaining is (1/2)⁴ = 1/16. Dividing 24 by 6 and taking 1/4 confuses the number of half-lives with the fraction remaining.

questions.stem: What is the decay constant of an isotope with a half-life of 6.0 hours?
questions.explanation: λ = ln 2/T½ = 0.693/6.0 ≈ 0.12 h⁻¹. Dividing the half-life by ln 2 gives 8.7, and 1/6.0 ≈ 0.17 h⁻¹ leaves out the ln 2.

questions.stem: On a graph of undecayed nuclei against time, the count falls from 1200 to 300 in 16 minutes. What is the half-life?
options: 4 minutes
16 minutes
12 minutes
8 minutes
questions.explanation: From 1200 to 300 is a fall to one-quarter, which takes two half-lives (1200 → 600 → 300). So 16 minutes is two half-lives, and the half-life is 8 minutes. Reading the time to fall by 900 nuclei as linear decay leads to the other answers.

questions.stem: Isotope X has a larger decay constant than isotope Y. Which statement is correct?
options: X and Y have the same half-life
X has a longer half-life only if its sample is larger
X has a shorter half-life than Y
X has a longer half-life than Y
questions.explanation: λ = ln 2/T½, so the decay constant and half-life are inversely related. A larger λ means a greater probability of decay per second, so the isotope decays faster. Half-life does not depend on sample size.

questions.stem: Why is technetium-99m widely used for medical imaging scans?
options: It emits beta particles that are stopped by the skin, so its radiation does not reach the patient's organs
It is not radioactive, so it can be injected safely and traced with an ordinary camera from outside
It emits gamma rays that escape the body, and its 6 hour half-life suits a scan without lingering
It emits alpha particles that destroy tumours, and its half-life of many years gives long-lasting treatment
questions.explanation: A tracer for scans must emit radiation that leaves the body and is weakly ionising, so gamma is ideal. A half-life of about 6 hours lasts long enough for the scan but leaves little activity afterwards. Alpha emitters inside the body would be highly damaging.

questions.stem: Smoke detectors commonly contain americium-241. Which property makes it suitable?
options: It emits neutrons that heat the air, and its long half-life keeps the alarm sensitive
It emits alpha particles that ionise the air in a chamber, and its long half-life lasts for years
It emits gamma rays that pass straight through smoke, and its short half-life keeps the detector safe
It emits beta particles that are absorbed by smoke, and its half-life matches the battery's life
questions.explanation: Alpha particles ionise the air in the detector, so a small current flows. Smoke absorbs the ions and lowers the current, triggering the alarm. Alpha particles are stopped by the casing and a few centimetres of air, and americium-241's long half-life means the source lasts the life of the alarm.

questions.stem: Which contribution to radio-medicine is Marie Curie known for?
options: Inventing PET scanning, and producing the first fluorine-18 tracers for hospitals
Explaining nuclear fission, and calculating the energy released by each split nucleus
Discovering polonium and radium, and organising mobile X-ray units in World War I
Discovering the neutron, and building the first nuclear reactor for medical isotopes
questions.explanation: Marie Curie, working with Pierre Curie, discovered polonium and radium in 1898, and radium was soon used to treat cancer. In World War I she organised mobile radiography units to X-ray wounded soldiers. The neutron was discovered by Chadwick, and fission was explained by Meitner and Frisch.

questions.stem: What does E = mc² mean for nuclear reactions?
options: Mass and energy are equivalent, so a decrease in mass is released as energy
Mass is always conserved, so energy can be created without changing mass
Energy is only released when a nucleus moves at the speed of light
Energy is always conserved, but the mass of the products is never different
questions.explanation: Special relativity shows that mass and energy are equivalent. In nuclear reactions the products have less total mass than the reactants, and the missing mass appears as energy, E = Δmc². Separate conservation of mass and of energy is replaced by conservation of mass-energy.

questions.stem: How much energy would be released if 1.0 g of matter were converted completely into energy?
questions.explanation: E = mc² = 1.0 × 10⁻³ × (3.00 × 10⁸)² = 9.0 × 10¹³ J. Leaving the mass in grams gives 9.0 × 10¹⁶ J, and forgetting to square c gives 3.0 × 10⁵ J.

questions.stem: Nuclear binding energy is:
options: the energy needed to separate a nucleus into its individual nucleons
the energy holding the electrons in their orbits around the nucleus
the energy released when a nucleus emits a single gamma photon
the kinetic energy of the nucleons as they move inside the nucleus
questions.explanation: Binding energy is the energy needed to pull a nucleus apart into separate protons and neutrons, and equally the energy released when the nucleus forms from them. It equals the mass defect multiplied by c².

questions.stem: A helium-4 nucleus has a mass of 4.001506 u. The masses of a proton and a neutron are 1.007276 u and 1.008665 u. What is its binding energy? (1 u = 931.5 MeV/c²).
options: 15.2 MeV
28.3 MeV
7.07 MeV
questions.explanation: The separate nucleons total 2 × 1.007276 + 2 × 1.008665 = 4.031882 u, so the mass defect is 4.031882 − 4.001506 = 0.030376 u. The binding energy is 0.030376 × 931.5 ≈ 28.3 MeV. Dividing by 4 nucleons gives the binding energy per nucleon, 7.07 MeV, not the total.

questions.stem: In the fusion reaction ²H + ³H → ⁴He + n, the masses are 2.014102 u, 3.016049 u, 4.002603 u and 1.008665 u. How much energy is released? (1 u = 931.5 MeV/c²).
options: 28.3 MeV
17.6 MeV
1.76 MeV
questions.explanation: Δm = (2.014102 + 3.016049) − (4.002603 + 1.008665) = 5.030151 − 5.011268 = 0.018883 u. E = 0.018883 × 931.5 ≈ 17.6 MeV, carried away mostly as kinetic energy of the neutron. 28.3 MeV is the binding energy of helium-4 alone.

questions.stem: Which equation correctly describes a fission reaction of uranium-235?
options: ²³⁵U → ¹⁴¹Ba + ⁹²Kr + 2n
²³⁵U + n → ¹⁴¹Ba + ⁹²Kr + 3n
²³⁵U + n → ¹⁴¹Ba + ⁹²Kr + n
²³⁵U + n → ¹⁴¹Ba + ⁹⁴Kr + 3n
questions.explanation: Nucleons must balance: 235 + 1 = 236 = 141 + 92 + 3. Charge also balances, as uranium (92) gives barium (56) and krypton (36). The other equations do not balance the nucleon number.

questions.stem: What is the difference between a controlled and an uncontrolled chain reaction?
options: Controlled: on average one neutron per fission causes another. Uncontrolled: more than one does
Controlled: no neutrons are released by fission. Uncontrolled: many neutrons are released by each fission
Controlled: fusion reactions only. Uncontrolled: fission reactions only, which always grow rapidly
Controlled: the fuel is natural uranium. Uncontrolled: the fuel contains no uranium-235 at all
questions.explanation: In a reactor, control rods and the design keep the average number of neutrons from each fission that go on to cause another fission at exactly one, giving a steady output. In a nuclear weapon this number is greater than one, so the number of fissions multiplies very quickly.

questions.stem: In a fission reactor, what are the functions of the moderator and the control rods?
options: The moderator absorbs neutrons to stop the reaction; control rods slow neutrons so they cause fission
The moderator carries heat to the turbines; control rods hold the fuel pellets in place
The moderator speeds up neutrons; control rods reflect neutrons back into the reactor core
The moderator slows neutrons so they cause fission; control rods absorb neutrons to regulate the rate
questions.explanation: Slow (thermal) neutrons are much more likely to cause fission of uranium-235, so a moderator such as water or graphite slows the fast neutrons released by fission. Control rods of neutron-absorbing material such as boron or cadmium are raised or lowered to keep the chain reaction steady. The coolant carries heat away.

questions.stem: What is the function of the coolant in a fission reactor?
options: To carry heat away from the core to produce steam
To absorb neutrons and shut down the chain reaction
To slow neutrons so they are more likely to cause fission
To provide the uranium fuel needed for each fission
questions.explanation: The coolant, often water, removes the heat released by fission from the reactor core and transfers it to make steam for the turbines. Absorbing neutrons is the job of the control rods; slowing them is the moderator's job.

questions.stem: What did Lise Meitner and Otto Frisch contribute to the discovery of nuclear fission?
options: They built the first nuclear reactor and achieved the first controlled chain reaction in it
They discovered the neutron by bombarding beryllium with alpha particles
They discovered radium and polonium in uranium ore and coined the term radioactivity
They explained Hahn and Strassmann's results as uranium splitting, and estimated the energy released
questions.explanation: Hahn and Strassmann found barium among the products when uranium was bombarded with neutrons. In 1939 Meitner and Frisch explained this as the uranium nucleus splitting in two, named the process fission, and used the mass defect and E = mc² to estimate about 200 MeV released per fission.

questions.stem: Why does nuclear fusion require extremely high temperatures and pressures?
options: Nuclei only have mass at high temperatures, and mass is needed for the strong force to act
Nuclei must collide fast enough to overcome electrostatic repulsion, and often enough to keep going
High temperatures split the nuclei into neutrons, which then join together to form heavier nuclei
High pressures turn the electrons into protons, which can then fuse with the nuclei around them
questions.explanation: Positive nuclei repel each other, and only at very high speeds, which means very high temperatures, can they get close enough for the strong force to bind them. High pressure and density make such collisions frequent enough to sustain the reaction, as in the core of a star.

questions.stem: Per kilogram of fuel, how does the energy released by nuclear fission compare with burning coal?
options: Fission releases about ten times more energy
Burning coal releases slightly more energy
They release about the same amount of energy
Fission releases millions of times more energy
questions.explanation: Fission of a uranium-235 nucleus releases about 200 MeV, millions of times more than the few electronvolts released per chemical bond in burning fuels or conventional explosives. Chemical reactions change electron arrangements, while nuclear reactions change the much more tightly bound nucleus.

questions.stem: Using a graph of binding energy per nucleon against mass number, which peaks near iron, why do both fission of heavy nuclei and fusion of light nuclei release energy?
options: Both produce nuclei further from iron, with lower binding energy per nucleon, so mass increases
Fission increases binding energy per nucleon, but fusion releases energy by destroying nucleons
Both release energy because they increase the total number of protons and neutrons
Both produce nuclei closer to iron, with higher binding energy per nucleon, so mass decreases
questions.explanation: Moving towards the peak near iron increases the binding energy per nucleon, so the products are more tightly bound and have less mass than the reactants. The mass defect is released as energy. Splitting iron or fusing it into heavier nuclei would absorb energy, which is the iron limit.

questions.stem: How does the neutron-to-proton ratio differ from binding energy as a measure of nuclear stability?
options: The ratio applies only to light nuclei, and binding energy applies only to nuclei heavier than iron
The ratio shows whether a nucleus lies in the band of stability; binding energy per nucleon, how tightly it is held
The ratio shows how tightly a nucleus is held; binding energy per nucleon shows whether it is radioactive
They measure the same thing, so a nucleus with a high ratio always has the highest binding energy
questions.explanation: A nucleus with too many or too few neutrons for its protons lies off the band of stability and will decay, by beta emission for example. Binding energy per nucleon measures how much energy, on average, holds each nucleon, which shows how energy changes in fission and fusion.

questions.stem: A positron is:
options: a photon with enough energy to cause ionisation in tissue
the electron's antiparticle, with the same mass and a charge of +1
a proton that has lost its charge and become a neutral particle
an electron moving at nearly the speed of light, with extra mass
questions.explanation: A positron has the same mass as an electron but the opposite charge, +e. It is emitted in beta-plus decay, and when it meets an electron the pair annihilates.

questions.stem: A positron and an electron, both nearly at rest, annihilate. What is produced?
options: Two gamma photons of 0.511 MeV each, travelling in opposite directions
One gamma photon of 1.022 MeV, travelling in the electron's direction
Two gamma photons of 1.022 MeV each, travelling in the same direction
A neutron, because the charges of the two particles cancel out
questions.explanation: The total rest mass, 2 × 9.109 × 10⁻³¹ kg, is converted into energy, 2 × 0.511 MeV. With almost no initial momentum, momentum conservation requires two photons travelling in opposite directions, each carrying 0.511 MeV. A single photon could not conserve momentum.

questions.stem: How does positron emission tomography (PET) produce an image of where a tracer collects in the body?
options: Positrons from the tracer annihilate with electrons, and detectors record the paired gamma rays to locate each event
The tracer emits alpha particles, which are photographed directly as they leave the patient's skin
Positrons travel out of the body to a detector, which records the point where each one leaves the skin
A beam of positrons is fired through the patient, and the shadows of the organs are recorded
questions.explanation: A positron-emitting tracer such as fluorine-18 in a glucose compound collects in active tissue. Each positron travels a tiny distance and annihilates, sending two 0.511 MeV gamma photons in opposite directions. A ring of detectors registering both photons at the same time pins down a line through the event, and many lines build up the image.
